prompt: Create a finished, landscape-format, artwork-led scientific infographic entitled “THE OCEAN’S CARBON PUMP”, directly on the canvas, not a poster mockup. A luminous, richly painted vertical ocean cross-section dominates: sunlit turquoise surface and delicate microscopic phytoplankton above, fading into a vast indigo deep sea. A graceful, branching downward drift of organic marine snow is the visual spine, dissolving into tiny particles and eventually the seabed. Use exquisitely observed, plausible organisms, subtle underwater light and suspended particulate texture, fine scientific ink and translucent watercolor-like shading. Integrate a few large, legible, unboxed close-up studies within the flowing scene, joined by curved fine leader lines: surface phytoplankton using light and dissolved CO₂ to build organic carbon; a zooplankton grazer eating phytoplankton and releasing a sinking fecal pellet; a close view of a loose aggregate of marine snow; deep-sea animals feeding on falling organic matter; a modest seabed deposition vignette. Use short exact labels “Photosynthesis”, “Phytoplankton”, “Zooplankton grazing”, “Fecal pellets”, “Marine snow”, “Carbon carried downward”, “Deep-sea food”, and “Some carbon stored in deep water and sediment”. Arrows clearly show the direction of sinking, without implying that all particles reach the bottom or that all carbon is permanently stored. Build a sophisticated asymmetric composition with generous open water and breathing room, varying the scale of studies; factual annotations flow organically through the art, not a rigid grid or detached boxes. Restrained ivory typography, strong hierarchy, readable spelling, no tiny paragraphs, no URLs, no logos or watermarks.

claims.claim: Sunlit phytoplankton use photosynthesis to convert carbon dioxide into organic carbon.
Phytoplankton can aggregate into sinking marine snow.
Zooplankton eat phytoplankton and produce carbon-containing fecal pellets that sink.
Sinking particles transport organic carbon from surface waters toward the deep ocean.
Marine snow provides food to deep-sea animals and seafloor organisms.
Some carbon reaches deep waters and sediments, where it can remain stored for long periods.

claims.claim: Milky seas are rare expanses of steady whitish marine bioluminescence visible at night.
Luminous bacteria are implicated, but their precise ecological relationships and conditions producing milky seas remain uncertain.
At high bacterial population density, chemical quorum sensing can trigger bacterial luminescence.
A 1985 sampled milky sea contained luminous bacteria associated with microalgae.
The glow may persist for days to weeks and drift with surface currents.
The VIIRS day-night band can detect the faint glow from orbit under favorable conditions; moonlight and clouds can complicate detection.
Unlike a milky sea’s steady glow, mechanically stimulated dinoflagellate bioluminescence typically flashes briefly.

claims.claim: Chrysoperla rufilabris is a green lacewing found in North America; humid habitats include irrigated crops and greenhouses.
Adults are pale green, with golden eyes, long antennae and transparent wings; adult size is roughly 12–20 mm.
Eggs are laid singly on silken stalks on foliage.
Larvae have three instars, legs and large curved paired mouthparts; they impale aphids and suck body contents.
Mature larvae spin a round silken cocoon; the pupa develops before the adult emerges.
Chrysoperla adults feed on nectar, pollen and honeydew while larvae are predators.
Generalized insect body plan: spiracles admit air into branching tracheae; the alimentary canal carries food and the ventral nerve cord runs along the body.
